title: Designing classes and interfaces
idea: Good class design gives each class one job, keeps data with the rules guarding it, and puts varying behaviour behind a small interface named for a role.

analogy.text: A hospital rota lists roles such as on-call surgeon, not names. Any qualified surgeon fills the slot, and each patient's chart travels with the patient.
analogy.breaks: A chart only records data; a Java record also refuses invalid values.

points: Requirement nouns suggest classes; verbs become methods on the class that owns the data.
Use a record for a value with rules, validated once in its constructor.
Extract an interface for behaviour that varies, and name it for the role.
Make classes final with private final fields unless designed for extension.

steps.caption: Requirement: book a patient with the clinician free earliest from a given hour. The nouns request, clinician and appointment are candidate types.
`Request` is a value with a rule: the hour must be 0 to 23. A record checks it once, at construction.
Clinicians keep hours differently. That variation becomes the `Availability` interface, named for the role it plays.
Each way of keeping hours is one small record. Each validates its own hours, so none can exist half-built.
The verb "find the earliest" lands on `FrontDesk`, which holds one or more clinicians by the interface only.
The desk only uses `Request` as a parameter: a dashed dependency, not a field.
The desk returns an immutable `Appointment`. A new kind of clinician adds one class and touches nothing else.

code.title: The problem
code.caption: Data in a bag of fields, rules in a `Utils` class. Half-built objects compile and run.

walk.text: `Clinician` is public fields plus a setter. Nothing says which fields a valid clinician needs.
Lee is created, given hours, and never named. The object is half-initialised but looks usable.
The booking rule lives in a utility class, far from the hours it reads.
Lee is free first, so the patient is booked with `null`: the bug surfaces far from its cause.
A public field accepts a shift that ends before it starts. Nothing can refuse it.

code.title: The fix
code.caption: Validated value objects, a role interface and a coordinator that depends only on that role.

walk.text: `Request` guards its hour in the compact constructor. No invalid request can exist.
`Availability` names a role. `FrontDesk` needs only a name and a first free hour.
Each way of keeping hours is its own record. Every field arrives in the constructor, checked.
The desk copies its list and rejects an empty one, so outside code cannot change its state.
It asks each clinician through the interface and keeps the earliest. No `if` on clinician kinds.
Wiring happens in `main`. Different hours pick different clinicians; a bad shift fails fast.

pitfalls: An interface for a class with one implementation adds files, not flexibility; wait for a second.
Public mutable fields let any caller break invariants; the bug shows up far from the cause.
A no-arg constructor plus setters lets half-built objects escape; a forgotten name prints `null`.

quiz.q: A new on-call clinician is free at any hour. What changes in the fixed design?
options: Add one class that implements Availability
Add a new method to the Availability interface
Make Request mutable so the clinician can set the hour
quiz.why: The desk talks to the `Availability` role only. An on-call class returns the requested hour from `firstFree`; no existing class changes.

takeaway: Keep data with its rules; hide varying behaviour behind a role interface.
